title: Ben-Menahem, Jewish Law (Int. Encyclopedia of the Social & Behavioral Sciences)

1.title: What Jewish law is, and how far it reaches
1.text: 'Jewish law' is the modern English epithet for HALAKHA, covering legal arrangements from biblical times to the present. Its foundational texts are the Torah (the Pentateuch) and the Talmud, and it is a normative system regulating ALL aspects of daily life, private and public — ritual, property, family, commercial and penal law, and the law of obligations; in the public domain the judiciary, taxation, communal regulations and constitutional law. The reach is the part to remember: although some segments are valid only in the land of Israel, THE JURISDICTION OF JEWISH LAW IS PERSONAL, NOT TERRITORIAL, and applies to Jews everywhere. It also makes a claim on humanity in general through the SEVEN NOAHIDE LAWS: the injunction to establish courts, and the prohibitions of blasphemy, idolatry, sexual transgressions, bloodshed, robbery, and eating flesh cut from a living animal. Today not all Jews accept its authority, though in previous millennia it was accepted as binding by Jews everywhere.

terms.def: Jewish law. A normative system covering ritual, property, family, commercial, penal and public law, whose jurisdiction is PERSONAL, not territorial.
The claim Jewish law makes on humanity in general: establish courts, and do not blaspheme, worship idols, commit sexual transgressions, shed blood, rob, or eat flesh cut from a living animal.

cards.q: Is the jurisdiction of Jewish law territorial or personal, and why does the distinction matter?
cards.a: Personal. Some segments of the halakha are valid only in the land of Israel, but the law applies to JEWS EVERYWHERE — which is what makes it workable in the diaspora, where there is no territory to attach it to.

cards.q: What claim does Jewish law make on non-Jews, and through which rules?
cards.a: Through the seven Noahide laws: the injunction to establish courts, and the prohibitions of blasphemy, idolatry, sexual transgressions, bloodshed, robbery and eating flesh cut from a living animal.

2.title: Why the law is felt to be 'democratic'
2.text: The role of halakha in post-biblical Jewish civilization cannot be overestimated: it is the force that held Jews together in Israel and the diaspora, and its study and interpretation are the PRIMARY FOCUS of Jewish intellectual endeavour, far overshadowing philosophy, homiletics and Kabbala. Study of the law is a paramount religious duty, to be carried out daily by laymen as well as scholars, and social and personal success are measured by achievement in studying it. Students are encouraged TO SPEAK THEIR MIND even against the received view, which lets individuals take part in the law's evolution — a participation limited to those actually studying Torah, but with a ripple effect that makes the community feel the law is an ONGOING ENTERPRISE RATHER THAN DICTATED FROM ABOVE. Most halakhic literature is written by individuals holding NO OFFICIAL POSITION, whose authority the community accepts for their erudition and integrity. And the cardinal decision-making principle is that THE LAW IS IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE MAJORITY VIEW.

cards.q: In what sense is Jewish law 'democratic, so to speak'?
cards.a: Study is a daily duty for laymen as well as scholars; students are encouraged to dissent from the received view, so individuals take part in the law's evolution; most halakhic literature is written by people holding no official position, accepted for their erudition and integrity; and the cardinal decision rule is that the law follows the MAJORITY view. The law feels like an ongoing enterprise rather than something dictated from above.

3.title: Periods and centres
3.text: The periods: the BIBLICAL period; the TALMUDIC period (1st century BCE – 5th century CE); the GEONIC period (6th–12th century); the EARLY AUTHORITIES, Rishonim (13th–16th century); and the LATER AUTHORITIES, Aharonim (17th century to the present). The four main geographic centres: the land of ISRAEL and BABYLONIA in the talmudic and Geonic periods, and later SFARAD — the Iberian peninsula and North Africa — and ASHKENAZ, Franco-Germany. Peripheral centres were largely under their influence. One methodological note: on the internal self-understanding, the Torah expresses a unified divine revelation, a claim unacceptable to contemporary biblical research — so by convention BIBLICAL RESEARCH IS TREATED AS A FIELD DISTINCT from research in Jewish law.
3.note: Ben-Menahem dates the periods slightly differently from the lecture (Geonim 6th–12th c. vs 650–1038, Rishonim 13th–16th c. vs about 1038–1563). For the exam the order and the century are enough; if asked for exact dates, follow the lecture.

cards.q: Name the four main geographic centres of Jewish legal activity.
cards.a: The land of Israel and Babylonia in the talmudic and Geonic periods; later Sfarad — the Iberian peninsula and North Africa — and Ashkenaz, Franco-Germany. Other centres were largely under their influence.

cards.q: Why is biblical research treated as a separate field from research in Jewish law?
cards.a: Because Jewish law's internal self-understanding is that the Torah expresses a unified divine revelation — a claim contemporary biblical research does not accept. Scholars therefore keep the two enterprises apart rather than making one depend on the other.

4.title: A legal system without the hallmark of a legal system
4.text: Jurisprudentially it is hard to see the periods and centres as ONE system, because the HIERARCHICAL INSTITUTIONAL STRUCTURE that is the hallmark of any legal system is absent. Jewish law developed although it was not the positive law of any state, and its central institution — the GREAT SANHEDRIN, the high court responsible for the system's uniformity and coherence — HAS NOT EXISTED FOR ABOUT 2,000 YEARS. Parts corresponding to modern criminal law have not been in force since. A tension between this reality and the ideal of a sovereign Jewish regime pervades the halakha, audible in the recurring phrase 'IN OUR DAY', which connotes the inferiority of the present. In the absence of a constitutive institution, four elements generate the law, themselves in tension: the RABBINICAL establishment in the yeshivot; the COMMUNAL establishment running civic affairs; THE MEMBERS of the community, who by adopting customs of their own force the establishment to reckon with them; and THE GENTILE SOCIETIES within which Jews live, whose mores always trickled down.

terms.def: The high court that kept Jewish law uniform and coherent. Gone for about 2,000 years — which is why Jewish law lacks the hierarchical structure that defines a legal system.

cards.q: Which hallmark of a legal system does Jewish law lack, and since when?
cards.a: A hierarchical institutional structure. Its central institution, the Great Sanhedrin — the high court responsible for the system's uniformity and coherence — has not existed for about 2,000 years, and parts corresponding to modern criminal law have not been in force since.

cards.q: With no constitutive institution, what generates Jewish law?
cards.a: Four elements in tension: the rabbinical establishment in the yeshivot; the communal establishment running civic affairs; the members of the community, who adopt customs the establishment must then reckon with; and the Gentile societies among which Jews live, whose mores trickled down.

cards.q: What does the recurring phrase 'in our day' express in halakhic literature?
cards.a: The tension between the present reality — no Sanhedrin, no sovereignty, only local validity — and the ideal of a sovereign Jewish regime with its own institutions. It connotes the inferiority of the present age.

5.title: De facto legal pluralism and the local authority
5.text: The direct source of the diversity of customs — amounting to a state of DE FACTO LEGAL PLURALISM — is that communities are guided by DIFFERENT halakhic authorities. Special status attaches to the local authority, the MARA DEATRA: the halakhic establishment validates a community's acceptance of the authority of its choice and recognises his decisions as binding on residents of that locale EVEN IF AT VARIANCE with prevailing views on the issue. At the same time no rigid schools of thought were created, and the works and rulings of every authority, whatever their place and time, remain relevant to the dialogue. So conceptually it is hard to call the centres one system, while SOCIOLOGICALLY the communities have no doubt that they are.

terms.def: The local halakhic authority, whose decisions bind the residents of his locale even where they diverge from prevailing opinion — the mechanism of Jewish legal pluralism.

cards.q: What is the mara deatra, and what does the institution produce?
cards.a: The local halakhic authority whom a community accepts. His decisions bind that locale even where they diverge from prevailing views — which produces a de facto legal pluralism, since communities follow different authorities.

6.title: Legislation and courts
6.text: Both organs of a legal system are present. LEGISLATION: whereas rulings of the Sanhedrin were universally valid, 'in our day' all legislation — TAKANOT — is of LOCAL validity only; nevertheless it is abundant and wide, covering civil and ritual law alike. THE JUDICIARY is highly developed, and the halakhic literature discusses at length: alternative dispute resolution such as arbitration and compromise; appointment of judges and their qualifications; payment for judging; the composition of the court; self-representation and representation by an agent; due process and equal treatment of both sides; the prohibition of any personal or financial interest of the judge in the case; fitness and examination of witnesses; rulings in writing; and publication, finality and implementation. How far the theory can be applied is a function of THE AUTONOMY GRANTED BY THE GENTILE AUTHORITIES. And resort to Gentile courts is treated as tantamount to RENOUNCING the halakha's authority.

cards.q: How far does takanot legislation reach 'in our day', and why?
cards.a: Only locally. Rulings of the Sanhedrin were universally valid, but with no Sanhedrin all legislation is of local validity — though abundant and covering the whole of civil and ritual law.

cards.q: How was resort to a Gentile court regarded?
cards.a: As tantamount to renouncing the authority of the halakha. Adjudicating within the Jewish court system, where possible, was zealously insisted upon.

7.title: The talmudic period and the divine/human distinction
7.text: The FORMATIVE era is the talmudic period, when the Mishna and Talmud were composed. The MISHNA is the compilation of the teachings of the TANNAITES, sages of Palestine in the first two centuries CE, arranged thematically over the whole of Jewish law. It then became the object of analysis by the AMORAITES, whose work went beyond commentary into the general culture: the Palestinian academies produced the JERUSALEM TALMUD around 400 CE, the Babylonian academies the BABYLONIAN TALMUD about a century later, with far more evident redaction. Talmudic law is premised on the revelation of the Torah to Moses at Sinai (the written law) and the accompanying ORAL revelation, later written down. Despite the divine origin the Torah was subjected to human scrutiny, and a distinction emerged between DEORAITA, deemed of divine origin, and DERABANAN, deemed of human origin. Rabbinic interpretation is not arbitrary but applies THE 13 EXEGETICAL PRINCIPLES — some fixing the meaning of the written law, others extrapolating new rules from it — though it is debated whether the sages really generated new law with them or used them as a literary device to attach new law to the biblical text (ASMAKHTA).

terms.def: Norms deemed of divine origin against those deemed of human origin — the basic distinction within talmudic law.
The suspicion that the 13 exegetical principles were sometimes a literary device for attaching a new rule to a biblical text rather than the means of deriving it.

cards.q: Who produced the Mishna and who the Talmuds?
cards.a: The Mishna compiles the teachings of the Tannaites, sages of Palestine in the first two centuries CE, arranged thematically. The Amoraites then analysed it: the Palestinian academies produced the Jerusalem Talmud around 400 CE, the Babylonian academies the Babylonian Talmud about a century later, far more heavily redacted.

cards.q: What do deoraita and derabanan distinguish?
cards.a: Norms deemed of divine origin (deoraita) from those deemed of human origin (derabanan) — the distinction that lets a law of divine origin still be subject to human scrutiny and elaboration.

cards.q: What are the 13 exegetical principles, and what is disputed about them?
cards.a: The principles by which the Torah is interpreted — some determining the meaning of the written law, others extrapolating new rules from it. It is disputed whether the talmudic sages actually generated new law with them, or used them as a literary device (asmakhta) to link a rule they already held to the biblical text.

8.title: Monetary law and ritual law
8.text: Beside the division into precepts between people (mitzvot bein adam lehaveiro) and precepts between the individual and the Almighty (mitzvot bein adam lamakom) — realms that are conceptually and practically interwoven, not separate — there is a second division that matters more in practice: MAMONOT, monetary law, against ISUR VEHETER, ritual law. Monetary law is deemed JUS DISPOSITIVUM and is therefore approached with GREATER FLEXIBILITY, so adjustments to changed circumstances can be made readily. And yet, despite that flexibility, in monetary disputes extreme caution is exercised before ruling that SOMEONE'S ASSETS ARE TO BE TAKEN AWAY.

terms.def: Monetary law against ritual law. Monetary law counts as jus dispositivum and is handled more flexibly — the 'secular' part of the halakha.

cards.q: Why is monetary law (mamonot) handled more flexibly than ritual law?
cards.a: Because it is deemed jus dispositivum — at the parties' disposal — so adjustments to changing circumstances can be instituted readily. Even so, extreme caution is exercised before ruling that someone's assets are to be taken away.

9.title: Layers, commentators and codes
9.text: The Babylonian Talmud holds its unique position because it is THE LATEST TEXT UNIVERSALLY ACCEPTED AS BINDING by the halakhic authorities — an authority established by the GEONIM, heads of the Babylonian academies after the Muslim conquest. From then on every legal discussion STARTS from the Babylonian Talmud's position, though it is not necessarily followed. Halakhic creativity accumulates in layers, IN TREE-RING FASHION: earlier contributions are always retained, so the evolution can be traced. Most of the literature is commentary on the Talmud — the preeminent commentator being RASHI, R. Solomon Yitzhaki (France, 1040–1105), and after him his students the TOSAFISTS. 'Legal codes' were compiled from time to time, especially in the Sfardic tradition: MAIMONIDES' Mishne Torah (Spain–Egypt, 1135–1204), the only completely comprehensive treatment of Jewish law; the ARBAA TURIM of R. Jacob b. Asher (c. 1269–1343); and the SHULHAN ARUKH of R. Joseph Caro (Israel, 1488–1575). The codes themselves then attracted commentaries known as 'ARMOR BEARERS', the codes being the 'knights'.

terms.def: R. Solomon Yitzhaki (France, 1040–1105), the preeminent commentator on the Talmud; his students are the Tosafists.

cards.q: Why does the Babylonian Talmud hold its unique position, and who established it?
cards.a: Because it is the latest text universally accepted as binding by the halakhic authorities — an authority established by the Geonim, heads of the Babylonian academies after the Muslim conquest. Every later discussion starts from its position, though it is not necessarily followed.

cards.q: Name the three great codes and their authors, with dates.
cards.a: Maimonides' Mishne Torah (Spain–Egypt, 1135–1204), the only completely comprehensive treatment of Jewish law; the Arbaa Turim of R. Jacob b. Asher (c. 1269–1343); and the Shulhan Arukh of R. Joseph Caro (Israel, 1488–1575).

cards.q: What does 'tree-ring fashion' describe about halakhic creativity?
cards.a: That it accumulates in successive layers with earlier contributions always retained, so the evolution of the law can be traced relatively easily rather than being replaced at each step.

10.title: Three levels: halakha, halakha lemaase, and the actual ruling
10.text: A duality that can mislead: the use of exact measurements and precise formulations (MIDOT VESHIURIM), the meticulous phrasing, the avoidance of abstractions like 'reasonable behaviour' and 'bona fide conduct', can make talmudic law look like a dry legalistic system deciding rights pedantically. That impression is fundamentally incorrect. The nature of the law AS IMPLEMENTED (halakha lemaase) cannot be inferred from its theoretical exposition (halakha) — and the distinction is found IN THE SOURCES THEMSELVES: 'one who inquires about practical law must state that he is inquiring for practical purposes… the practical takes precedence'. So any description must separate law intended for implementation from theoretical law. For the talmudic period the former rests on episodes, precedents and rulings in the Talmud; for the post-talmudic period the RESPONSA literature is far more reliable than other genres. The responsa began in the Geonic period and have flourished since — some 250,000 of them have accumulated, part electronically indexed by the Bar Ilan Responsa Project — alongside the surviving communal records (PINKASEI HAKEHILOT) and collections of legal instruments.

terms.def: Law intended for implementation, as against halakha, the theoretical exposition. The distinction is drawn by the sources themselves, and the practical inquiry takes precedence.
The surviving records of the judicial and legislative activity of Jewish communities — a source for the law as actually applied.

cards.q: Name the three levels of law Ben-Menahem distinguishes.
cards.a: Theoretical law (halakha); law intended for implementation (halakha lemaase); and the concrete ruling, which will occasionally diverge even from the law intended for implementation. The first two usually overlap.

cards.q: Which source tells you what Jewish law actually WAS in practice after the talmudic period, and how much of it survives?
cards.a: The responsa literature — legal opinions issued in answer to queries from courts with cases before them — which began in the Geonic period. Some 250,000 responsa have accumulated. Communal records (pinkasei hakehilot) and collections of legal instruments are a further source.

11.title: Judicial deviation from the law
11.text: An accepted truism of western legal thinking is that a judge's ruling must accord with the law — grounded in a well-defined body of norms, known in advance, applied to the case. The Babylonian Talmud does NOT fit that model: THE JUDGE HAS THE POWER TO DEVIATE FROM THE LAW and to base his ruling on extra-legal considerations. The tradition in the name of R. Eliezer b. Jacob puts it flatly: 'I heard that the beit din punishes… not according to the Torah'. In most cases there is no discrepancy; WHAT IS SIGNIFICANT IS NOT THE FREQUENCY OF DEVIATION BUT THAT IT IS AN OPTION. The judge does not see himself as constrained by the rules, and where the circumstances justify departing from them he need not hesitate. This does not sanction arbitrary deviation: when he deviates he does so to impose THE SPIRIT OF THE TORAH, traditionally seen as not reducible to a set of rules. Over time this became the norm, and although judges did not always feel comfortable deviating, THEIR AUTHORITY TO DO SO WAS NEVER QUESTIONED.

cards.q: May a halakhic judge depart from the law, and what makes the power significant?
cards.a: Yes — he may deviate and rule on extra-legal considerations ('the beit din punishes not according to the Torah'). What is significant is not how often it happens but that it IS AN OPTION: the judge does not regard himself as bound by the rules. The deviation is not arbitrary; it is made to impose the spirit of the Torah, which is held not to be reducible to rules.

12.title: Governed by men, not by rules
12.text: The heart of the article, and the answer to the exam question that quotes it. The western ideal is 'GOVERNED BY RULES, NOT BY MEN', and it rests on the idea that a litigant is one who CLAIMS HIS DUE, not one who SEEKS SUCCOR: his claim presupposes the court's submission to a well-defined, publicly known body of norms and a rule entitling him to win. A litigant before a rabbinical court claims NO entitlement to a favourable ruling even where a rule seems to give him one, because the judge may depart from the rule and decide as he sees fit — so the litigant's status is that of one SEEKING THE COURT'S AID. Hence the converse adage, 'GOVERNED BY MEN, NOT BY RULES'. And this explains the absence of three almost universal institutions: BINDING PRECEDENT is beside the point where a decision may be ad hoc; COURTS OF APPEAL exist to secure uniformity and the supremacy of rules, which are not priorities here; and EQUITY COURTS are a corrective for the law's inflexibility, and no such corrective was needed where the judge is already free. The judge's freedom rests on judging being a religious precept — 'you judge not for men, but for the Lord' — and such a system can work only in a community that accepts the judge as a spiritual leader and role model, not merely an expert technocrat.

cards.q: In what sense is Jewish law 'governed by men, not by rules'?
cards.a: Because the judge may depart from the rule and decide as he sees fit, a litigant before a rabbinical court claims no entitlement to a favourable ruling even where a rule appears to give him one. He is not one claiming his due but one SEEKING THE COURT'S AID — the reverse of the western ideal, where the court is bound by publicly known norms.

cards.q: Which three near-universal legal institutions are absent from Jewish law, and why?
cards.a: Binding precedent — pointless where a decision may be ad hoc. Courts of appeal — they exist to secure uniformity and the supremacy of rules, which are not priorities here. Equity courts — a corrective for the law's inflexibility, unnecessary where the judge is already free to deviate.

cards.q: What does the judge's freedom rest on, and what does the system require of the community?
cards.a: On judging being a religious precept, the fulfilment of a divine calling — 'you judge not for men, but for the Lord' — which frees him from rules formulated in human language. The system can thrive only in a community that accepts the judge as a spiritual leader and role model rather than an expert technocrat hired to administer the law.

13.title: Jewish law in the State of Israel, and the non-Orthodox
13.text: With the return to Zion, non-religious thinkers proposed founding Jewish life in Israel on Jewish law, and at the beginning of the 20th century the term MISHPAT IVRI, Hebrew law, was coined for the part of the halakha corresponding to civil and criminal law, EXCLUDING its ritual aspects. The agenda never gained acceptance; it was reintroduced by national-religious circles as statehood approached, and again failed. Today Israeli positive law recognises Jewish law as the law of the state only in FAMILY LAW, adjudicated in state-run rabbinical courts, and in a few isolated laws on religious observance — otherwise its influence on Israeli law is MINUSCULE, although rabbinical courts unconnected to the state thrive, as they always did in the diaspora. From the 19th century the hegemony of the rabbinical reading was challenged: the REFORM movement rejected the halakha altogether, while the CONSERVATIVE movement sought to accelerate halakhic change and to articulate the role of conscience — and, given that the halakha is pluralistic anyway, the Conservative–Orthodox divide is sociologically significant but involves NO divide about accepting the halakha's authority.

cards.q: How far does Jewish law count as the law of the State of Israel today?
cards.a: Only in family law, adjudicated in state-run rabbinical courts, and in a few isolated laws on religious observance. Otherwise its influence on Israeli law is minuscule — though rabbinical courts unconnected to the state thrive, as they did throughout the diaspora.

cards.q: How do the Reform and Conservative movements stand towards the halakha?
cards.a: Reform rejected the halakha altogether. Conservative Judaism sought to accelerate halakhic change and to articulate the role of conscience — but does not differ from Orthodoxy about the halakha's AUTHORITY, so the divide is sociological rather than one about acceptance of the law.
